subject: health
title: How My Body Works and Stays Well
standards: Michigan Health Practice 3: Information and Resource Seeking
Michigan Health Practice 5: Self-Management and Goal Setting
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Personal Health and Wellness
essential_question: How do my body systems and my daily habits work together to keep me well?

topic_content.name: body systems working together
key_points: Systems cooperate: the respiratory system takes in oxygen, the circulatory system carries it, and muscles use it.
The digestive system breaks food into fuel the blood can deliver.
The skeleton supports and protects; the skin is the first barrier against germs.
Because systems are connected, a habit like sleep or hydration affects several at once.
topic_content.scenario: Running upstairs leaves you breathing hard with a fast heartbeat. Which systems are responding, and why do both change together?

topic_content.name: germs and how illness spreads
key_points: Bacteria and viruses are different: antibiotics work on bacteria and do nothing to viruses.
Germs spread by droplets from coughs and sneezes, by direct contact, by contaminated surfaces, and through food and water.
Someone can pass on an illness before they feel ill themselves.
Breaking one link in the chain — washing, covering, staying home, cleaning surfaces — stops the spread.
topic_content.scenario: One person in a class has a stomach bug on Monday and six do by Friday. Trace the likely routes and name the two changes that would help most.

topic_content.name: handwashing and respiratory etiquette
key_points: Soap works by breaking up the outer layer of many germs, which is why scrubbing beats a quick rinse.
Twenty seconds, covering palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, and nails.
Sanitizer is a stand-in when soap is unavailable, and does not work well on visibly dirty hands.
Cough or sneeze into your elbow or a tissue, throw the tissue away, then wash.
topic_content.scenario: Someone rinses their hands with water for three seconds and says they washed. Explain, using how soap works, why that is not enough.

topic_content.name: dental and skin care
key_points: Brush twice daily for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, and clean between teeth.
Plaque is a bacterial film; left alone it causes decay and gum disease.
Skin needs washing, sun protection, and clean cuts covered to keep germs out.
Adult teeth are permanent, so damage now lasts.
topic_content.scenario: A friend brushes once a day and never cleans between their teeth, and their gums bleed. Explain what is likely happening and what to change.

topic_content.name: sleep quality and routines
key_points: Around 9 to 12 hours a night is typical at this age.
Sleep consolidates memory and learning, and supports mood, growth, and immunity.
Blue light and stimulating content near bedtime delay falling asleep.
A consistent schedule works better than catching up at weekends.
topic_content.scenario: Someone sleeps five hours on school nights and twelve on Saturday, and still feels tired. Explain why the weekend does not fix it.

topic_content.name: checkups and staying well
key_points: Routine checkups find problems early, before they are felt.
Vaccines teach the immune system to recognize a germ safely in advance, which protects the person and people who cannot be vaccinated.
Bring questions to appointments; you are allowed to ask about your own body.
Medical decisions are made by guardians and health professionals, not by children or by the internet.
topic_content.scenario: A friend says checkups are pointless when you feel fine. Give two reasons that is not right.

home_connection: With a guardian, find out where the household keeps its first-aid supplies and the doctor or clinic contact details. This is optional. No purchase, account creation, photograph, measurement, or private disclosure is required.
performance_task: Design a prevention routine that explains what each step protects, why it works, and when adult or professional help is needed.
adapted_alternative: Diagrams may be replaced with text descriptions, tactile models, or spoken explanation. Any routine step a learner cannot perform independently is planned as an adult-supported step, which counts fully.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Household hygiene items only. No medical device, thermometer reading, or body measurement is used.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Check soap, sanitizer, and dental products against any known allergy before use.

subject: health
title: Balanced Eating, Hydration, and Active Living
standards: Michigan Health Practice 1: Self-Awareness and Analyzing Influences
Michigan Health Practice 5: Self-Management and Goal Setting
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Balanced Eating and Physical Activity
essential_question: How can I plan food, water, and movement in a way that fits my body, my day, and my family?
topics: what different foods do for the body
media messages about food and bodies

topic_content.name: what different foods do for the body
key_points: Carbohydrates are the body's main everyday fuel, including for the brain.
Protein builds and repairs muscle, skin, and blood.
Fats support the brain and help absorb some vitamins; the body needs them.
Fruit and vegetables supply vitamins, minerals, and fiber that keep digestion working.
No single food does everything, which is why range matters more than any one item.
topic_content.scenario: A lunch is bread, butter, cheese, and an apple. Which jobs are covered? What could be added without calling the lunch bad?

topic_content.name: food allergies and cross-contact safety
key_points: An allergy is an immune reaction; an intolerance is a digestive one, and allergies can be life-threatening.
Cross-contact is when a trace transfers by a shared knife, board, toaster, or unwashed hand — a trace is enough.
Labels must flag major allergens; "may contain" means a real risk.
Signs needing an adult immediately: swelling of lips, face or throat, widespread rash, wheezing, or difficulty breathing.
Never talk someone into eating something they have said they cannot eat.
topic_content.scenario: A peanut-butter knife was rinsed and used for jam on a friend's sandwich. The friend is allergic to peanuts. Is that safe? Explain what should have happened.

topic_content.name: media messages about food and bodies
key_points: Ads, influencers, and filters present altered images, not real bodies.
Bodies genuinely differ in size and shape, and healthy comes in many of them.
Claims that a food is "clean", "guilt-free", or "bad" are marketing, not nutrition.
Content that makes you feel worse about your body is worth unfollowing; talk to a trusted adult if it keeps happening.
topic_content.scenario: A post promises a snack that will "fix your body in two weeks" and shows a before-and-after photo. Name three reasons to distrust it.

topic_content.name: building balanced meals and snacks
key_points: A workable pattern: half the plate fruit and vegetables, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, plus dairy or an alternative.
Pairing carbohydrate with protein tends to keep energy steadier than carbohydrate alone.
Snacks are a normal part of the day at this age.
Plans have to survive real life: budget, time, and what is actually in the house.
topic_content.scenario: Redesign a snack of crackers alone so it lasts longer through an afternoon, using only cupboard staples.

topic_content.name: hydration through the day
key_points: Water carries nutrients, controls temperature, and cushions joints.
Pale straw-colored urine suggests you are drinking enough; dark yellow suggests not.
Needs rise with heat, illness, and activity.
Sugary and caffeinated drinks are not everyday hydration.
topic_content.scenario: Someone drinks only at meals, plays sport at midday in summer, and gets afternoon headaches. Suggest a plan.

topic_content.name: reading a simple food label
key_points: Ingredients are listed by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.
The allergen information is usually emphasized in bold or a separate statement.
Serving size matters: the numbers on the label describe one serving, not the whole pack.
A label describes what is in a food; it does not tell you whether the food is allowed or forbidden.
topic_content.scenario: On one label sugar is the second ingredient and the pack holds four servings. What does that tell you, and what does it not tell you?

home_connection: With a guardian, look at one food label from the cupboard and find the ingredients list and any allergen warning. This is optional. No purchase, account creation, photograph, measurement, or private disclosure is required.
performance_task: Build a week of flexible meal, snack, hydration, and movement options with substitutions for allergies, preferences, culture, and budget. No calorie counting, dieting, weight goal, or body measurement is used.
adapted_alternative: Planning may use pictures, dictation, sorting cards, or a spoken walkthrough. Learners with allergies, medical diets, religious or cultural food practices, or limited food access plan with the foods actually available to them, and any example may be substituted.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Clean, empty food packaging or printed labels. No cooking with heat is required.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Kitchen or table setting with an adult present for any food handling.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Active-living examples only; the learner chooses intensity and may rest at any point.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Guardian confirms every food example, label, and any handling against household allergies, intolerances, medical diets, and dietary practices. No tasting is required to complete any lesson.

subject: health
title: Emotional Health and Managing Stress
standards: Michigan Health Practice 1: Self-Awareness and Analyzing Influences
Michigan Health Practice 2: Social Awareness, Relationship, and Communication Skills
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Mental and Emotional Health
essential_question: How can I manage strong feelings and know when to reach for support?

topic_content.name: emotion vocabulary and intensity
key_points: Precise words give better options: disappointed, overwhelmed, resentful, anxious, relieved, content.
Intensity matters — irritated, angry, and furious call for different responses.
Two feelings can be present at once, such as excited and nervous.
Naming a feeling accurately tends to reduce its intensity.
topic_content.scenario: Someone says only "I am fine" while slamming doors. Offer three more accurate words and say what each would suggest doing.

topic_content.name: help-seeking and trusted supports
key_points: Reaching out is a skill, not a weakness or a failure.
Build a support list: guardians, a relative, a teacher, a coach, a school counsellor or nurse.
Get help promptly when a feeling stops you eating, sleeping, or going out, when it lasts for weeks, or when anyone talks about harming themselves.
If someone mentions hurting themselves, tell a trusted adult immediately — that is never a secret to keep.
If the first adult does not respond, keep telling until someone acts.
topic_content.scenario: A friend says they feel hopeless and asks you to promise not to tell. What do you do, and what do you say to your friend?

topic_content.name: stress signals and triggers
key_points: Stress shows up in the body — headaches, stomach aches, tight muscles, disturbed sleep.
It shows up in behavior too — snapping, avoiding, rushing, or going quiet.
A trigger is the situation that sets it off; noticing patterns lets you plan ahead.
Some stress before a challenge is normal and can help you focus.
topic_content.scenario: Every Sunday evening one learner gets a stomach ache that clears by Monday afternoon. What might the trigger be, and how could you check?

topic_content.name: change, loss, and difficult feelings
key_points: Moving, a family change, or the death of a person or pet all bring grief, and grief is not an illness.
Grief arrives in waves rather than in tidy stages, and there is no correct schedule.
Routines, talking, and remembering all help; so does being allowed to feel bad for a while.
A trusted adult should know when a hard feeling is not easing.
topic_content.scenario: A classmate's dog died two weeks ago and they were laughing yesterday but tearful today. Is that normal? What could a friend say?

topic_content.name: coping and regulation strategies
key_points: Slow breathing with a longer out-breath lowers the body's alarm response.
Grounding by naming what you can see, hear, and touch brings attention back to the present.
Movement, water, daylight, and sleep are underrated regulators.
Match the strategy to the setting — some work in a classroom, some only at home.
Strategies work better when practiced before you need them.
topic_content.scenario: Build a toolkit for someone who gets overwhelmed in noisy places and cannot leave the room. What actually fits that constraint?

topic_content.name: self-talk and mindset
key_points: Self-talk is the running commentary in your head, and it can be checked for accuracy.
"I cannot do this" becomes "I cannot do this yet", which describes the situation more truthfully.
Mistakes are information about the method, not verdicts about the person.
Speak to yourself the way you would speak to a friend in the same position.
topic_content.scenario: After a hard test someone thinks "I am useless at math." Rewrite that thought so it is both kinder and more accurate.

home_connection: With a guardian, agree one signal you can use at home that means "I need a few minutes". This is optional. No purchase, account creation, photograph, measurement, or private disclosure is required.
performance_task: Build a coping-strategy toolkit matched to different fictional stress scenarios, plus a help-seeking plan. Private reflection is never required to be shared or stored.
adapted_alternative: Coping strategies may be movement-based, still, sensory, verbal, or silent, and each learner selects strategies their body and setting allow. Scenario responses may be pointed to, chosen from options, drawn, spoken, or written.

guardian_safety_review.environment: Quiet indoor space with a break space available.

subject: health
title: Relationships, Boundaries, and Conflict Repair
standards: Michigan Health Practice 2: Social Awareness, Relationship, and Communication Skills
Michigan Health Practice 6: Advocacy and Health Promotion
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Healthy Relationships
essential_question: How do I speak up for myself, respect others, and repair a relationship after conflict?
topics: body autonomy, consent, and unsafe requests

topic_content.name: assertive, respectful communication
key_points: Passive gives in, aggressive attacks, assertive states your need and respects theirs.
A clear frame: "When ___ happens, I feel ___, and I would like ___."
Tone, volume, and body language carry as much as the words.
Being assertive does not guarantee you get what you want; it makes being understood far more likely.
topic_content.scenario: A friend keeps borrowing things without asking. Write a passive, an aggressive, and an assertive version, and say why the third is better.

topic_content.name: body autonomy, consent, and unsafe requests
key_points: Your body belongs to you; you decide about hugs, tickling, and touch, including with family.
The parts covered by a swimsuit are private. Use correct anatomical names — they make you easier to understand and to believe.
No one should touch, look at, photograph, or ask to see your private parts, except a doctor or nurse checking your health with your guardian present, or a caregiver helping you when you need help.
Unsafe requests most often come from someone already known and trusted, not from a stranger — so the rule applies to everyone.
Bribes, threats, and "this is our secret" are warning signs.
If it happens it is never your fault, whatever you did, accepted, or agreed to earlier. Tell a trusted adult and keep telling until someone helps.
topic_content.scenario: An adult a family knows well asks Sam to sit on their lap and keep it "just between us." Name every warning sign, and say exactly what Sam should do.

topic_content.name: listening and perspective-taking
key_points: Active listening: face the person, let them finish, then summarize before replying.
Two people can experience the same event differently and both be reporting honestly.
Asking a genuine question beats assuming a motive.
Understanding someone is not the same as agreeing with them.
topic_content.scenario: Two friends give opposite accounts of an argument. How would you find out more without deciding who is lying?

topic_content.name: conflict resolution and repair
key_points: Cool down first — nothing useful gets settled mid-anger.
State the problem as a behavior, not as a character flaw.
Look for a solution both can live with, not for a winner.
A real repair names the specific action, apologizes for it, and changes something afterwards.
topic_content.scenario: Two friends both think the other started it and neither will speak. Write the first three steps towards repair.

topic_content.name: bullying and cyberbullying response
key_points: Bullying is deliberate, repeated, and directed at someone struggling to stop it.
Cyberbullying follows people home, spreads fast, and leaves a record.
Keep the evidence, do not retaliate, block and report, and tell a trusted adult.
Bystanders shift outcomes by refusing to join in, supporting the person afterwards, and reporting.
topic_content.scenario: A group chat is sharing an unkind edited photo of a classmate. List what you do, in order, and what you do not do.

topic_content.name: inclusion and respect for differences
key_points: People differ in ability, culture, language, faith, family shape, and interests.
Exclusion can be quiet — never being picked, never being asked — and still does harm.
Inclusion often means changing the activity rather than asking the person to cope.
Asking someone what would help beats guessing on their behalf.
topic_content.scenario: A game needs fast running and one classmate uses a wheelchair. Redesign the game so they are genuinely playing, not just present.

home_connection: With a guardian, review who is on your list of adults you could tell if something felt wrong. This is optional. No purchase, account creation, photograph, measurement, or private disclosure is required.
performance_task: Write and rehearse assertive communication and conflict-repair scripts for fictional situations, including a bystander response plan.
adapted_alternative: Scripts may be spoken, signed, typed, drawn as a comic, or acted with figures. Role-play is optional and may always be replaced by describing what a character should say and why.

guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: None. This unit covers personal-safety and consent rules; guardians may wish to preview it.

subject: health
title: Safety, Injury Prevention, and Digital Life
standards: Michigan Health Practice 4: Decision Making and Problem Solving
Michigan Health Practice 3: Information and Resource Seeking
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Safety and Injury Prevention
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Substance Use and Misuse
essential_question: How do I prevent harm and respond well when something goes wrong?
topics: emergency response and calling for help
medicines, household chemicals, and substance safety
basic first aid and when to get an adult

topic_content.name: injury prevention and protective gear
key_points: Most injuries at this age are predictable and preventable: falls, collisions, and road incidents.
A helmet sits level, two fingers above the eyebrows, snug strap, and is replaced after a hard impact.
Gear only works when it fits and is actually worn.
Checking the surface, the equipment, and the space first prevents more injuries than reacting well afterwards.
topic_content.scenario: Before skating at a new park, list the checks you would do on gear, surface, and surroundings.

topic_content.name: emergency response and calling for help
key_points: Call 911 in the United States for fire, serious injury, someone not breathing, or a crime in progress.
Give what happened, the full address, and your name; stay on the line until told otherwise.
Check the scene is safe before approaching — do not become a second person who needs help.
Know your address and a guardian's number by heart; a locked phone can still call emergency services.
Prank calls take help away from someone who genuinely needs it.
topic_content.scenario: You find an adult collapsed and unresponsive at home and you are alone. Give the exact sequence, including what you say on the call.

topic_content.name: medicines, household chemicals, and substance safety
key_points: Medicine is given by a trusted adult only, at the right dose, and is never shared.
Prescription medicine belongs to one named person; taking someone else's is dangerous.
Alcohol, nicotine, vapes, and other drugs affect a developing brain more than an adult one.
Vapes are not harmless water vapor; most contain nicotine, which is addictive.
Never taste or sniff an unlabeled substance. If someone has swallowed something, tell an adult at once — speed matters.
topic_content.scenario: An older student says vaping is "just flavored air" and offers one. Give two accurate facts in reply and say what you do next.

topic_content.name: basic first aid and when to get an adult
key_points: Small cut: wash with clean water, apply gentle pressure, cover.
Burn: cool under running water for around 20 minutes, then get an adult. Never use ice, butter, or cream.
Nosebleed: sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose.
Always get an adult for head injuries, bleeding that will not stop, breathing trouble, a suspected broken bone, or any loss of consciousness.
Your job is to recognize and fetch help, not to treat someone yourself.
topic_content.scenario: A friend falls, hits their head, and seems dazed and confused. What do you do, and what do you not do?

topic_content.name: online privacy and personal information
key_points: Personal data — full name, address, school, birthday, phone, location, passwords — stays private.
Photos can carry location data and can be copied and re-shared beyond your control.
Privacy settings help but never make something truly private.
A digital footprint lasts; assume anything posted could be seen by a guardian or a future school.
topic_content.scenario: A quiz app asks for your birthday, school, and first pet's name to "find your spirit animal." What is actually being collected, and why does it matter?

topic_content.name: recognizing unsafe requests and refusing
key_points: Warning signs: secrecy, flattery, gifts, urgency, isolating you, or asking you to break a family rule.
Online grooming often begins friendly and moves slowly towards secrets and images.
A refusal is short and repeated; you do not owe an explanation, and you may simply leave or log off.
No one is allowed to ask for a photo of your body, and you never have to send one; the answer is always no, and you always tell a trusted adult.
Telling is always the right thing to do, and none of it is your fault, even if you already replied or already agreed.
topic_content.scenario: Someone met in a game says they are 11, sends a gift code, asks for a photo, and says not to tell. Identify every warning sign and give the full response.

home_connection: With a guardian, check that everyone in the household knows the home address and one emergency contact number by heart. This is optional. No purchase, account creation, photograph, measurement, or private disclosure is required.
performance_task: Create a safety and refusal plan covering an activity, an online situation, and an emergency, reviewed and confirmed by a guardian.
adapted_alternative: First-aid content is taught as recognition and when-to-get-help, not as independent treatment. Any hands-on step may be observed, described, or demonstrated by the adult instead of performed by the learner.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: First-aid kit inspected with an adult; helmet or protective gear if the learner uses wheels or sport equipment.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor setting, plus a guardian-supervised outdoor area if chosen. Water and fire content is planning and discussion only.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: No learner performs first aid on another person, tests a hazard, or enters water as part of this unit. Gear fitting is adult-supervised.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: If the first-aid kit is reviewed, check adhesive, latex, and antiseptic contents against known allergies.

subject: health
title: Decisions, Goals, and Health Advocacy
standards: Michigan Health Practice 4: Decision Making and Problem Solving
Michigan Health Practice 5: Self-Management and Goal Setting
Michigan Health Practice 6: Advocacy and Health Promotion
Michigan Health Practice 1: Self-Awareness and Analyzing Influences
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Community and Environmental Health
essential_question: How do I make a sound decision, set a goal I can reach, and advocate for health beyond myself?
topics: influences from peers, family, and media
setting and tracking a personal health goal

topic_content.name: a step-by-step decision process
key_points: Name the decision precisely, because a vague question gets a vague answer.
List options, including ones nobody has suggested.
Weigh likely consequences for you and for others, short term and longer term.
Decide, act, then review whether it worked — reviewing is what improves the next decision.
Safety decisions always include a trusted adult.
topic_content.scenario: Friends want to bike along a busy road with no bike lane to reach a park faster. Work the process and justify your decision.

topic_content.name: checking sources and spotting misinformation
key_points: Ask who wrote it, when, and what they gain if you believe it.
Prefer health organizations, hospitals, and qualified professionals over anonymous posts.
Cross-check a claim in at least two independent places.
Warning signs: miracle cures, "what doctors will not tell you", urgency, and a product attached to the claim.
Sponsored content is an ad even when it looks like advice.
topic_content.scenario: Two pages disagree about whether a supplement helps children concentrate. One sells it. Describe how you decide what to believe.

topic_content.name: influences from peers, family, and media
key_points: Influence is often invisible: placement, repetition, and who is shown using a product.
Peer influence can push either way, towards risk or towards good habits.
Family habits shape defaults such as meals, bedtime, and activity.
Noticing an influence is what gives you the option to choose differently.
topic_content.scenario: A learner suddenly wants a drink they have never tried. Trace three possible influences and say how you would test which was strongest.

topic_content.name: setting and tracking a personal health goal
key_points: A workable goal is specific, realistic, and has a visible first step.
"Drink water with each meal" beats "be healthier", because you can tell whether you did it.
Track the action, not your body — never weight, size, or appearance.
Expect to miss some days; a plan that survives a missed day is a better plan.
topic_content.scenario: Turn "get fitter" into a goal a nine-year-old could actually start tomorrow and check on Friday.

topic_content.name: community health helpers and access
key_points: Community health includes clinics, school nurses, pharmacists, dentists, libraries, and food programmes.
Access is not equal: cost, transport, language, and disability all get in the way.
Knowing what exists locally is itself a health skill.
Helping someone reach a service is a genuine form of advocacy.
topic_content.scenario: A family new to the area does not know where to get a child's vaccination. Who could help, and how would you find out?

topic_content.name: advocating for a healthier community
key_points: Advocacy is speaking up for a change with a reason and an audience in mind.
A strong message states the problem, gives evidence, and makes one clear ask.
Direct it at someone who can actually act — a school, a city council, a store.
Children's advocacy works, especially when it is specific and polite.
topic_content.scenario: Your park has no shade and no water fountain. Draft the one clear ask, name who receives it, and give the evidence you would include.

home_connection: With a guardian, pick one household health habit worth improving and talk about what would make it stick. This is optional. No purchase, account creation, photograph, measurement, or private disclosure is required.
performance_task: Set a private-safe personal health goal with a plan and a progress check, and produce an advocacy piece supported by a reliable source. Goals may not target body weight, body size, or appearance.
adapted_alternative: Goal tracking may be a checklist, a spoken check-in, a drawing, or an adult-recorded note. The advocacy piece may be a poster, letter, slide, spoken message, or described plan. No public posting, publication, or performance is required.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: None beyond writing or digital tools.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor setting; supervised internet use when sources are compared online.
